opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that the number by itself tells you almost nothing. "Ten million hours" sounds impressive, but in robotics the hours are not interchangeable the way tokens kind of are in language. So when I see a number like that, I start asking a few questions.

First, what is the data actually of? Is it robot data, meaning a real robot with real actions recorded at every timestep, or is it human video, or teleoperation through some proxy device, or simulation? Those are very different things. Ten million hours of egocentric human video is useful for something, maybe learning what the world looks like or what people tend to do, but it doesn't directly tell a robot what torques to apply or how hard to squeeze. The further the data is from the robot's own body and action space, the more you're betting on transfer, and transfer is still very much an open problem.

Second, what is the diversity? You could collect ten million hours of a robot folding the same towel on the same table, and I'd guess the model mostly learns to fold that towel on that table. What matters much more is how many distinct environments, objects, tasks, lighting conditions, and embodiments are covered. A smaller dataset that is broad can be worth much more than a huge one that is narrow and repetitive. A lot of hours are often just the boring middle of a long task, the arm moving through free space, and those frames carry very little information.

Third, what is the quality, and specifically, how much of it shows interesting behavior? For manipulation, the valuable moments are the contact-rich parts, the failures and recoveries, the slightly unusual situations. If the data is all clean, successful demonstrations, the policy never sees what to do when something goes wrong, and in the real world things go wrong all the time. So I'd want to know whether there's corrective data, whether there are failures, and whether the actions are precise and well synchronized with the observations. Bad timestamps or noisy action labels can quietly ruin a lot of hours.

And then the last test, which is really the only one that counts: does training on it actually move the needle on robots doing things in new settings? Does performance keep improving as you add more of it, or does it plateau quickly? If someone can show me a scaling curve where more of their data reliably gives better generalization on held-out tasks and held-out environments, that's convincing. If all they have is the headline number, I'd treat it as marketing until proven otherwise.

So my short answer is: I don't judge it by the hours. I judge it by how close it is to the robot's real action space, how diverse it is, how much of it contains the hard and informative moments, and whether there's evidence that it actually scales into capability.

r001.rationale: The response says the hour count alone tells you almost nothing and explicitly asks what kind of data the dataset contains, distinguishing robot data, human video, teleoperation, and simulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I do when I see "10 million hours" is ignore the number. Hours are the easiest thing to inflate and the least informative thing to know. A camera bolted above a conveyor belt running for a year gives you 8,000 hours of almost nothing. So the headline figure tells me about the marketing team, not the dataset.

What I actually want to know breaks into a few questions.

First, what is the unit of value? For robot learning, the unit is not an hour, it's a successful, well-labeled trajectory of a task with some variation in it. So I ask: how many distinct tasks? How many distinct objects, scenes, lighting conditions, embodiments? If the 10 million hours are 50 tasks repeated in three labs, that's a small dataset wearing a big coat. If it's 5,000 tasks across hundreds of environments, now we're talking.

Second, where did it come from? Teleoperation with a real robot, human video, simulation, or some mix? Each has a very different value per hour. Teleop on the target hardware is gold but expensive, so if someone claims 10 million hours of that, I immediately ask about the budget, because the arithmetic usually doesn't close. Human egocentric video is cheap and plentiful but has an embodiment gap you have to pay for later. Sim can be effectively infinite, which is exactly why counting it in hours is a bit silly.

Third, what's the action and state annotation like? Pixels alone are much less useful than pixels plus synchronized proprioception, end-effector pose, gripper state, and ideally some notion of task success. A huge pile of video with no actions is closer to a pretraining corpus than a robot dataset. Both are useful, but they're not the same product and shouldn't be priced the same.

Fourth, I want to see the failure modes. Did they keep failed episodes? Are they labeled? Did they filter aggressively, and if so, did they throw away the hard cases? A dataset that's all clean successes teaches a policy that panics the moment anything goes wrong.

And then the real test, which is boring but decisive: take a known model, train it on a slice of this data, and measure downstream performance against the same model trained on an existing open dataset. If 10 million hours doesn't beat, say, a few thousand hours of carefully curated data on the tasks you care about, the number was noise.

So my short answer is: I value a dataset by diversity, annotation quality, and provenance, and I verify by training on it. The hour count is just the thing that gets you to open the email.

r001.rationale: The response says to ignore the headline hour count and judge the dataset by its trajectory diversity, provenance, and annotation quality.

astra-6.text:
I’d ask what those 10 million hours actually contain. Hours measure volume, but they don’t tell you how much a robot can learn from the data.

Is it video of people doing things, simulated robot experience, or real robot interaction? Do you have synchronized observations and actions? What tasks, environments, and robot types does it cover? Ten million hours of repetitive motion could be less useful than a much smaller dataset with diverse, well-recorded examples relevant to the task you care about.

Then I’d look at failures and recovery. Does the dataset only show successful demonstrations, or does it show what happens when an object slips, the robot misses, or the environment changes? That matters because operating a robot means responding to consequences, not just reproducing a sequence.

Ultimately, I’d judge it by a controlled experiment: with the same model and training budget, does adding this dataset improve success on held-out tasks and unfamiliar environments? Does it reduce the amount of new robot data you need? Until you can demonstrate that, ‘10 million hours’ is a claim about scale, not a demonstration of value.

r001.rationale: The response says hours measure volume but not what a robot can learn, then recommends examining what the data contains and its relevance rather than judging by total hours alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d first ask what those 10 million hours actually contain. Are they robot interactions, human videos, simulation, or the same trajectories repeated in different forms? An hour of footage isn’t necessarily an hour of useful training signal.

Then I’d look at diversity and quality. What tasks, environments, objects, and robot embodiments does it cover? Are actions and sensor streams synchronized? Does it include failures and recovery, or only successful demonstrations? Ten million hours of a narrow, repetitive task may be less valuable than a much smaller dataset with broad, well-recorded interactions.

But the decisive test is what it does for the robot. With the model and training budget held comparable, does adding this data improve success on unfamiliar tasks and environments? Does that improvement hold up on a real robot? I’d judge the dataset by those gains, and by the cost of making it usable—not by the number of hours in the headline.

r001.rationale: The response says to inspect what the hours contain and notes that the headline hour count alone does not establish value.
